newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi leader says Hutu rebels cannot win war.
newsitem.headline: Burundi leader says Hutu rebels cannot win war.

text.p: Hutu rebels cannot win Burundi's ethnic guerrilla war but economic sanctions are helping them, army-backed President Pierre Buyoya said on Thursday.

Major Buyoya, installed in a coup last July 25, said in an interview the embargo was killing the peace process. He repeated his readiness to negotiate with rebels despite accusing their leader of taking part in a 1993 "genocide" of Buyoya's minority Tutsi tribe.
"(The rebels) cannot win. Especially where the civil war is also a kind of ethnic war. Peace can only come through negotiations," Buyoya told Reuters.
The regional sanctions clamped on landlocked Burundi on July 31, to punish the coup by the overwhelmingly Tutsi army, will be reviewed at a summit on October 12 in Arusha, Tanzania.
Buyoya said he had not yet received an invitation but hoped to explain his peace plan to regional leaders and persuade them to lift the trade and transport embargo.
"We think we have fulfilled all the conditions and we want the sanctions to be lifted," he said.
His regime has unbanned political parties, agreed to restore parliament and pledged to enter negotiations with Leonard Nyangoma and leaders of other armed Hutu factions.
These were the three main conditions set by the pro- sanctions countries.
Buyoya accused Nyangoma of indiscriminate killing of civilians and said he was among Hutu leaders who planned and ordered what he termed the genocide of Tutsis in late 1993.
"What can I think of a man like that?" Buyoya asked.
Thousands of Tutsis were killed by Hutus in reprisal for the assassination by Tutsi soldiers of Burundi's first freely- elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, in October 1993.
Asked why he would accept talks with Nyangoma, a man he considered a murderer, Buyoya replied: "Maybe you cannot chose your negotiating partner."
The 46-year-old Buyoya was president before, taking power in a barracks coup in 1987 before accepting multi-party elections and losing against Ndadaye, a Hutu, in June 1993.
Ndadaye's murder plunged Burundi into an ethnic war that has killed about 150,000 people.

Buyoya said on Thursday the last three years had shown the failure of Western-style politics here and his government would stage a national debate to find a system which guaranteed democracy and security for both majority and minority.
Tutsis have always held the levers of power in Burundi but Hutus are 85 percent of the population and the rebels say their days as underdogs will soon be over.

The government believes the rebels are avoiding talks because they reckon the blockade on all imports and exports can help them gain a military victory against an under-supplied army. But the rebellion is gaining strength and is even trying to set up parallel administrations, diplomatic sources say.

The army, over 20,000-strong after a recruitment drive this year, is hard-pressed to protect the capital Bujumbura and Tutsi communities, defend strategic installations and try to keep most main roads safe from ambush during daylight hours.
Buyoya defended the army against allegations of repeated massacres of Hutu civilians as reprisals for rebel operations.
Citing past wars in Algeria and Vietnam, where ironically regular armies were defeated, Buyoya said there were always "some abuses and some kind of indiscipline" when troops fought guerrillas.
